children.text: As discussed in the previous page, how we categorize the world tells us as much about our own categorical systems as it does about the world itself. Among the species that share this planet with us, ocean mammals have been particularly associated with “playfulness.” Play, in this sense, is one of the many ways
cetaceans especially come to be read as “more-like-us”, compared to other species.

When we look for animals that seem like us, two groups keep surfacing: primates and cetaceans. Primates hold that likeness through evolutionary genealogy. Chimpanzees and bonobos are our closest living relatives, sharing a common ancestor with humans roughly six to seven million years ago and some 98–99% of our DNA. Cetaceans hold it differently, through behaviour and affect rather than ancestry: they are known for being emotionally intelligent, highly social creatures who form tight family units and durable bonds, and who seem, watching them, to be having something like fun.

Dolphins, for example, are known for their playful antics. They demonstrate many traits of play, from acrobatics to games with objects. Similarly, other marine animals, like seals and otters, engage in playful behaviours. These activities serve various purposes, from honing skills to social bonding. Animal behaviourists explores play in marine animals to understand their cognitive abilities and social dynamics.

There is a deep history to search for beings like us beneath the water. Sailors told of mermaids and singing sirens, and whalers and naturalists wrote of mysterious creatures of the abyss that possess extraordinary capabilities. From SETI to CETI: John Lily, the "Order of the Dolphin", and using AI to understand animals

Among the people who have been dedicated to see ocean mammals as "more like us", was John Lilly, an American neuroscientist and physician who had already made his name studying the brain. He pioneered the isolation tank as a tool for sensory-deprivation research, before turning his attention to dolphins in the late 1950s, founding the Communication Research Institute to study them in the U.S. Virgin Islands. Lilly pushed that intuition much further, and much more literally, than earlier whale-song enthusiasts had. Convinced from the 1950s onward that dolphin vocalizations amounted to a language, he pursued direct communication with them through isolation tanks, shared living quarters, and eventually LSD, administered to dolphins and to himself, hoping chemistry might close the gap between two kinds of mind. His influence outlasted the specifics of his method. When a small group of scientists convened at Green Bank in 1961 to found what became the search for extraterrestrial intelligence, they named themselves, half-jokingly, the “Order of the Dolphin” in his honor — reasoning that learning to listen to a mind as alien as a dolphin’s was good practice for learning to listen to one from another planet.

That premise, that an alien mind might be decoded if we listened carefully and built the right tools, has outlived Lilly’s own career, which drifted toward the fringe of serious science. It resurfaces today in projects like Project CETI (the Cetacean Translation Initiative), which applies machine learning to the patterned clicks, or “codas,” of sperm whales, hoping to uncover something like grammar and eventually build an AI system that can respond in kind. The CETI, in mimicry, takes after the name of SETI (“Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence”). Aside from Project CETI, Earth Species Project and similar initiatives are making the same bet across other species, from elephants to birds, training large language models on animal vocalizations much as they’re trained on human text using cryptography and neural networks.
